courseDescription: A hands-on, concept-first journey into Python. Moving from basic syntax to professional-grade scripts, this course builds fluency through deep conceptual understanding and a cumulative project: building a fully-tested, API-integrated automation tool. You will progress from writing your first program to designing modular libraries and class-based systems, all while adhering to industry-standard best practices.
targetLearner: Aspiring developers and professionals seeking to master Python through a logic-first approach, transitioning from basic programming mechanics to robust software engineering practices.

projects.project_description: Build a professional-grade command-line tool that fetches real-time weather data from an API, processes historical trends, and generates formatted reports. The project evolves from a simple script into a robust, object-oriented application with full error handling and automated tests.
projects.final_deliverable: A complete, pip-installable Python package including a CLI entry point, a data-processing class library, JSON/CSV export functionality, and a pytest-driven test suite.

units.title: Python Foundations
units.description: Establish the fundamental mechanics of code, covering variables, basic arithmetic, control flow logic, and string manipulation. This unit focuses on building the mental model of how Python executes instructions.

lectures.title: Getting Started
lectures.description: This lecture introduces the execution environment of Python and the basic building blocks of any program: data types and mathematical operations.

sessions.title: Running Python and Your First Program
sessions.description: You will learn how to interact with the Python interpreter and the basic syntax of the print statement. By the end of this session, you will be able to run scripts and understand the basic flow of a computer program. This provides the necessary environment to begin your journey toward building scripts and automation tools.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this lecture series by demystifying the 'black box' of programming. The central idea is to shift the student's perspective from being a passive consumer of software to being its director. I will start by conceptualizing the Python Interpreter as a tireless translator that sits between our human thoughts and the silicon reality of the computer hardware. This establishes the 'Why' before the 'How': we learn Python because it is a language designed for human readability, yet powerful enough to control complex machine logic.

To move from concept to action, we introduce the Read-Eval-Print Loop (REPL). On the virtual whiteboard, I will illustrate the three-step cycle: the machine receives a command (Read), calculates the result (Eval), and shows us what happened (Print), before waiting patiently for the next instruction. This 'conversation' is the fastest way to build intuition. When we type 'Hello World', the core lesson isn't the text itself, but the syntax requirements—the specific use of quotes to signal 'data' versus 'commands' and the parentheses that tell the 'print' function to execute. This is a critical moment to preempt the common beginner mistake of forgetting quotes; I explain that without them, Python looks for a variable or a command that doesn't exist, leading to our first encounter with a SyntaxError.

Once the learner feels comfortable with the immediate feedback of the REPL, we must pivot to the concept of 'Scripts'. While the REPL is a great conversation, it is ephemeral—it forgets everything once closed. To build real tools, we need memory and persistence. I will visualize a .py file as a 'script' or a recipe that the computer follows from top to bottom. This transition is vital because it introduces the linear flow of execution. We will write a multi-line script, demonstrating that Python processes commands in a strict sequence. This is where we emphasize that the computer is literal-minded: it won't jump to line 5 until line 1 is finished.

To solidify this, the session concludes with a transition from simple output to intentional messaging. I will guide the learner to create a script that outputs a short narrative or a sequence of steps. This isn't just about printing text; it's about the learner realizing they have gained the power to orchestrate a sequence of events. By the end of this session, the learner should not just know how to run a script, but feel the structural difference between a 'one-off command' and a 'stored program,' setting the stage for the variables and data types that will populate these programs in the next session.

tasks: Run a simple 'Hello World' script in the Python REPL.
Create and execute a .py file that prints multiple lines of text.

sessions.title: Values, Variables, and Types
sessions.description: This session covers how Python stores data in memory using variables and the fundamental types including integers, floats, and strings. You will understand how to name variables and how Python's dynamic typing system works. This is essential for managing the state of your application as you build toward the CLI calculator project.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by de-mystifying the 'magic box' of a variable. Instead of starting with syntax, I will draw a high-level conceptual metaphor: memory as a vast warehouse of labeled containers. I'll explain that while the computer sees memory as hexadecimal addresses, Python allows us to give these locations human-friendly names. The core intuition to drive home here is that a variable is not the value itself, but a name that points to a specific spot in memory. This distinction is crucial because it sets the stage for understanding object references later in the course. I'll demonstrate this by 'tagging' an imaginary value on the board, showing how the label (the variable name) can be moved from one 'box' to another.

Next, we transition into the mechanics of naming. I will present this as a 'social contract' between the programmer and the computer. I'll start by listing illegal names—those starting with numbers or containing spaces—to explain why the interpreter cannot parse them (the ambiguity problem). Then, I'll move into Pythonic 'Snake Case' conventions. The goal here is to emphasize that code is read more often than it is written. I will challenge the learners to identify why a variable named 'x' is inferior to 'user_age' in a real-world script. By the time we finish this section, learners should view naming not just as a syntax rule, but as the first step in writing self-documenting code.

We then dive into the 'dynamic' nature of Python's typing system. I'll introduce the big three for this stage: Integers, Floats, and Strings. Rather than just listing them, I will show them as different 'shapes' that fit into different 'slots.' I'll explain that in Python, the type lives with the value, not the variable name. This 'Dynamic Typing' is a double-edged sword; I'll illustrate this by re-assigning a variable that held a number to a string and asking the class to predict what happens. This prevents the common misconception held by those coming from C or Java that a variable is 'locked' to a specific type forever, while simultaneously warning them about the confusion this flexibility can cause in larger programs.

To solidify the concept of types, we will use the `type()` function as a diagnostic tool. I'll frame this as the 'interrogator'—a way to peek under the hood when the behavior of a program feels inconsistent. I'll pose a puzzle: 'If I have "5" and 5, are they the same?' This leads into a demonstration of how a string of digits is functionally distinct from a mathematical integer. We will perform a quick check where we assign various data types and verify them, helping learners realize that Python is always tracking these identities behind the scenes.

Finally, we wrap up by connecting these concepts to the upcoming CLI calculator project. I'll explain that variables are the 'state' of our application—they hold the numbers the user types in and the results we calculate. Without variables, our program would have 'amnesia' and lose every calculation as soon as it's performed. I'll finish by having the learners practice declaring variables for a hypothetical invoice system, ensuring they can correctly choose between floats for currency and strings for names, which builds the foundational habit of data modeling.

tasks: Assign different data types to variables and use the type() function.
Identify valid and invalid variable names based on Python conventions.

sessions.title: Numbers and Arithmetic
sessions.description: You will explore the mathematical capabilities of Python, including addition, subtraction, multiplication, and various types of division. You will be able to perform complex calculations using operators like modulo and exponentiation. Mastering these operations is the direct foundation for building the logic of your Stage 1 calculator project.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this public lecture style delivery, we transition from the abstract storage of data to the active manipulation of numeric values. The central thesis of this session is that Python is not just a storage bin for data, but a powerful computational engine. We begin by visualizing the standard arithmetic operators—addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division—as the primary tools of this engine. It is crucial here to establish the distinction between 'float' and 'integer' results in division. I will explain that in Python, a single forward slash (/) always returns a float (e.g., 4 / 2 is 2.0), which is a common source of confusion for those expecting whole numbers. This allows us to introduce floor division (//) as the 'integer-only' counterpart, stripping away the remainder to maintain strict data types.

Moving deeper into the 'grammar' of numbers, we focus on the Modulo operator (%), which I characterize as the 'remainder finder.' Rather than just defining it as a percent sign that does math, I will use a visual analogy of a clock or a repeating cycle. For example, if we have 13 objects and group them into boxes of 5, the modulo operator tells us what’s left over (3). This is a foundational concept for later logic, such as checking if a number is even or odd or creating periodic resets in software loops. To solidify this, I'll pose a quick mental challenge: 'What is 10 % 3 vs 3 % 10?' This helps students understand that the operator is directional and depends entirely on how many times the divisor fits into the dividend.

Next, we elevate the discussion to Exponentiation (**) and the order of operations. It is important to emphasize that Python follows standard mathematical precedence (PEMDAS/BODMAS), but we must be explicit about how it handles negative numbers and powers. I will illustrate how parentheses are the programmer's 'safety net,' ensuring that logic is executed in the intended sequence rather than relying on the interpreter's default rules. This prevents the 'logic bugs' that often plague early calculator scripts where a simple square root or complex tax calculation yields the wrong result because of a missing set of brackets.

We conclude by contextualizing these tools within the Stage 1 CLI Calculator project. Instead of just solving abstract math problems, I will present a scenario—such as calculating the fuel efficiency of a vehicle or the compound interest on a loan. This shift from 'syntax' to 'application' forces the learner to translate a real-world problem into a Python expression. I'll highlight the common pitfall of trying to perform math on strings (e.g., '5' + 5), reminding them that arithmetic only works once the data is in its proper numeric container. This bridge ensures they aren't just memorizing symbols, but are learning how to build the functional core of an application.

tasks: Calculate the remainder of a division using the modulo operator.
Write expressions to solve basic physics or finance word problems.

sessions.title: Expressions and Type Conversion
sessions.description: This session explains how Python evaluates complex expressions and how to manually convert between different data types like strings and integers. You will understand how to handle user input which always arrives as text. This allows you to process raw data into numerical formats suitable for calculation.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing the computer as a rule-following machine that needs absolute clarity, introducing the concept of an 'Expression' as any chunk of code that evaluates to a single value. The goal is to move the learner beyond seeing code as static lines and instead seeing it as a dynamic process of reduction. I will illustrate this by writing a complex mathematical expression on the board and physically 'collapsing' it step-by-step, showing how Python follows a strict hierarchy of operations (PEMDAS). The core insight here is that understanding operator precedence isn't about memorizing a table, but about predicting how the computer will simplify logic before it acts on it.

Next, we tackle the 'Type Wall.' I will pose a scenario where we try to add a string of text to a number—for example, adding a price of '10' (received as text) to a $5 tax. This allows me to explain that while humans see '10' and 10 as the same thing, Python’s memory architecture sees a sequence of characters versus a binary magnitude. I will draw two different shaped containers on the board to visualize why they cannot be merged without a bridge. This leads naturally into 'Type Casting' or conversion. I'll demonstrate the int(), float(), and str() functions, framing them as 'translators' that allow data to cross the border between different internal representations.

A critical moment in this session is the 'Input Trap.' Since the input() function always returns a string, beginners often get frustrated when their math results in errors or unexpected string concatenation (like '5' + '5' resulting in '55'). I will demonstrate this specific failure live. This serves as a teaching moment for the 'Sanitize and Convert' pattern: we never trust raw data from the outside world. I will show how to wrap the input function inside a conversion function, explaining this 'nested' logic as a pipeline where data flows from the keyboard, through the translator, and finally into a variable we can actually use for math.

To solidify these concepts, we will engage in a 'Precedence Prediction' exercise. I will write three ambiguous expressions on the board—mixing division, multiplication, and type conversion—and ask the learners to guess the final type and value before we run the code. This exercise is designed to reveal misconceptions about how Python handles integer versus float division during evaluation. We wrap up by connecting these skills back to our Unit project: if we are building a calculator, every button press is a string that must be methodically transformed into a number before the 'plus' sign can do its job. This ensures the learner understands that conversion isn't a chore, but the foundational step of all data processing.

tasks: Convert a string input into an integer to perform arithmetic.
Predict the output of mixed-type expressions following operator precedence.

lectures.title: Control Flow
lectures.description: Move beyond linear execution by learning how to make decisions and repeat actions based on conditions.

sessions.title: Booleans and Comparison
sessions.description: You will learn about the Boolean data type and the comparison operators that produce True or False values. You will be able to write logical tests that check for equality, inequality, and magnitude. This provides the 'brain' for your programs to evaluate the state of data before acting.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the lecture by shifting the perspective from 'how to calculate' to 'how to decide.' Introduce the Boolean data type not just as a variable type, but as the fundamental binary state of computing—True or False. Explain that while strings and integers store data, Booleans store the outcome of an evaluation. Draw a distinction between the assignment operator (=) and the equality operator (==) on the board immediately; this is the most common pitfall for beginners. Visualizing the single '=' as a 'bucket filler' and the double '==' as a 'balance scale' helps ground this conceptual difference before they even write a line of code.

Transition into comparison operators by framing them as questions we ask the computer. Instead of listing them as syntax, demonstrate them through the lens of magnitude and identity. Use a simple number line on the board to illustrate <, >, <=, and >=. A critical teaching point here is the inclusion of the 'boundary' in 'greater than or equal to.' Show how changing a single character from '>' to '>=' can shift the logic of a program entirely, which is the perfect moment to introduce the concept of 'off-by-one' errors. This builds the 'mechanical intuition' mentioned in the course architecture by showing how small syntax choices impact program logic.

Introduce Logical Operators (and, or, not) as the 'connective tissue' of complex decision-making. Rather than using dry truth tables initially, use a real-world scenario like 'Is it the weekend AND is it sunny?' to explain 'and', and 'Do I have an umbrella OR is it not raining?' for 'or'. This 'concept-first' approach allows learners to grasp the philosophy of compound logic without getting bogged down in formal notation. Explain that 'not' is a logical inverter, flipping the state, which is a powerful tool for writing cleaner code—for instance, checking if a list is NOT empty rather than explicitly checking its length.

During the practice moment, challenge the learners to check if a number is within a specific range, like 10 to 20. This exercise is designed to reveal a common syntax mistake: beginners often try to write '10 < x < 20' (which Python actually supports, but many languages don't) versus the explicit 'x > 10 and x < 20'. By having them write it out the long way first, they learn how the computer evaluates each side of the 'and' independently. This deepens their understanding of the 'brain' of the program, ensuring they see logical tests as individual expressions that resolve to a single True or False value before the program moves forward.

tasks: Use comparison operators to check if a number is within a specific range.
Combine multiple conditions using logical 'and', 'or', and 'not'.

sessions.title: if, elif, and else
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to branch your code execution using conditional blocks. You will learn to handle multiple scenarios within a single program flow. This is a core requirement for creating a calculator that chooses different operations based on user selection.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this public lecture, we pivot from the binary logic of 'True vs False' to the architectural reality of 'Branching Paths.' I will begin by visualizing the concept of code execution not as a straight line, but as a railway switch. The primary goal here is to instill the intuition that conditional blocks are the decision-making engine of any software. I’ll start with the basic 'if' statement, framing it as a gatekeeper: if the condition is met, the code enters a private block of execution; if not, it simply skips it. It is vital to emphasize Python's use of indentation here, as this is the physical manifestation of scope—a concept that beginners often struggle with. I'll explain that the colon and the subsequent shift in the margin are not just stylistic choices, but instructions telling Python which lines belong to that specific decision.

Once the binary choice is established, I will introduce the 'else' clause. The core idea here is the 'Guaranteed Execution'—that no matter what happens, one path will be taken. I’ll use a simple real-world analogy: if it's raining, take an umbrella; otherwise, take sunglasses. This leads naturally into the 'elif' keyword, which is frequently misunderstood as just another 'if'. I will clarify that 'elif' represents a linked chain of mutual exclusivity. If the first condition is met, the rest of the chain is ignored. This is a critical efficiency concept; we don't want the computer checking if a number is less than 10 if we've already confirmed it is less than 5. I will visualize this as a series of filters in a funnel, where the data drops through until it hits the first matching layer.

To move into the application phase, we will tackle the temperature categorization exercise. Instead of just writing code, I'll walk through the logic of 'order of operations' in conditions. A common pitfall is overlapping ranges—for example, checking if a temperature is 'greater than 0' before checking if it is 'greater than 30.' I will demonstrate why the more specific condition must usually come first. This teaches the learner to think about the hierarchy of logic. We will then transition to the concept of nesting, using a login validation scenario. Here, I'll show how an 'if' inside another 'if' creates a dependency—you can't check a password if the username doesn't exist yet. This introduces the idea of 'Stateful Logic,' where the context of the program changes as it moves deeper into nested blocks.

Finally, we will connect these concepts back to our Unit 1 project: the CLI calculator. I will frame the 'if-elif-else' structure as the 'Brain' of the calculator. This is the moment where the learner realizes they can now translate a user's intent (like typing '+') into a specific mathematical action. I will wrap up by warning against 'Arrow Code'—the practice of nesting too deeply, which makes code unreadable. The key takeaway for the learner should be that while conditionals allow for complexity, the goal is always to keep the logic as flat and readable as possible, ensuring that the code's path remains predictable and easy to debug.

tasks: Write a script that categorizes a temperature as 'Hot', 'Cold', or 'Mild'.
Create a nested conditional structure to validate user login logic.

sessions.title: While Loops
sessions.description: You will understand how to repeat a block of code as long as a condition remains true. You will learn to manage loop termination to avoid infinite execution. This enables your programs to handle ongoing tasks like a continuous command-line interface.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this public lecture style delivery, we transition from static decision-making to the dynamic concept of persistence. I begin by visualizing the limitation of the 'if' statement: it is a one-time gate. To illustrate this, I draw a fork in the road on the whiteboard. An 'if' statement lets you choose a path once, but then you move on. A 'While Loop', however, is a 'looping path' that returns you to the gate for as long as the condition remains True. This conceptual shift—moving from code that 'runs' to code that 'persists'—is the cornerstone of creating interactive software like game loops or command-line interfaces.

I then introduce the 'Three Pillars of a Loop' to prevent the common pitfall of the infinite loop. On the board, I label these as Initialization, Condition, and Update. I explain that for a loop to be useful, it must have a starting state, a rule that decides when to keep going, and a mechanism that changes the state so that the rule eventually becomes False. Without the 'Update' step, the program enters a state of 'immortality' that crashes the system. I demonstrate this with the '1 to 10' example, showing how a variable `i` must be incremented each time the loop body executes, otherwise, the 'gate' will never close.

To deepen the intuition, we move into the 'Sentinels' concept—loops that are not bound by a fixed number of repetitions but by a specific event. I describe the 'While True' pattern as a powerful but dangerous tool. I frame it as a 'Patient Listener' that waits for a specific signal, such as the user typing 'quit'. I draw a logic flow showing the code hitting a `break` statement, which acts like an emergency exit door, instantly bypassing the loop logic. This is crucial for students to understand that control flow isn't just about following tracks; it's about knowing how to jump off the tracks when a specific condition is met.

Finally, we engage in a practice moment where we attempt to build a simple interactive shell. I ask the learners to reflect on why a standard 'if' statement would fail to handle a user who keeps entering the wrong password. This reveals the true utility of the while loop: it creates a program that can handle human unpredictability. By the end of this session, the learner should view the While loop not just as a syntax for repetition, but as a mechanism for creating an environment where the program stays 'alive' and responsive to the outside world.

tasks: Write a loop that prints numbers from 1 to 10.
Create a loop that keeps asking for input until the user types 'quit'.

sessions.title: Loop Patterns: Counters, Accumulators, and Sentinels
sessions.description: This session introduces professional patterns for managing loops, such as keeping track of counts and totaling values. You will be able to solve common programming problems like averaging a list of inputs. These patterns are essential for building robust data-processing logic in later units.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by conceptualizing the 'State of the Loop.' In a public lecture style, I will frame this session not as a syntax lesson, but as the moment where we transition from merely repeating actions to making those actions productive. I'll draw a distinction between a 'dumb loop' that just repeats a task and an 'intelligent loop' that remembers its history. This sets the stage for our first pattern: the Counter. I will visualize a scoreboard in the student's mind—a variable sitting outside the loop, initialized at zero, that is updated incrementally. The critical insight here is the 'Variable Lifetime': if the variable is defined inside the loop, it dies and resets every iteration. We must define it before the loop to maintain a persistent state across cycles.

Moving to the Accumulator pattern, I will contrast it with the Counter. While a counter says 'how many,' an accumulator says 'how much.' I'll use the metaphor of a rolling snowball or a piggy bank. Instead of adding 1, we add a dynamic piece of data—like a user's input—to a running total. This is where I introduce the common pitfall of the 'Empty Accumulator'—forgetting to initialize a sum to 0 or a product to 1. I will challenge the learners to think about what happens if we start a multiplication accumulator at 0, revealing the logic error before they ever type a line of code. This illustrates why the starting value must be the identity element of the operation being performed.

Next, I will introduce the Sentinel pattern as the 'Professional Exit Strategy.' Up until now, loops often ran for a fixed number of times. I will frame the Sentinel as a special value that signals the end of a process, like the 'End of File' or a user typing 'quit.' The core concept here is the 'Guard Duty'—the loop condition constantly checks for this specific value. To prevent the 'Off-by-One' error or the 'Stale Data' problem, I will demonstrate the 'Prime-the-Pump' technique: asking for the first piece of data before the loop starts, and then asking again at the very end of the loop body. This ensures that the Sentinel value itself is never accidentally processed as valid data (e.g., adding the number -1 to a sum when -1 was actually the quit command).

To bridge these concepts into a cohesive system, we will conduct a mental walkthrough of a 'Statistics Engine.' I will explain how a Counter and an Accumulator work in tandem to calculate an Average: the Accumulator tracks the sum of values, while the Counter tracks how many values were entered. I will pose a rhetorical question: 'What happens if the user quits immediately?' This introduces the necessity of defensive programming—checking if the counter is zero before dividing. This reinforces the idea that programming is as much about anticipating empty states as it is about processing data.

Finally, we will transition to the practice phase. The exercise of tracking negative numbers forces students to combine the Counter pattern with 'if' logic from previous sessions, moving them toward algorithmic thinking. The second task of building an integer accumulator builds their confidence in managing state variables. Throughout this, I will emphasize that these aren't just Python tricks; they are universal architectural patterns used in everything from low-level drivers to high-level financial software, preparing them for the more complex data containers they will encounter in Unit 2.

tasks: Implement a counter that tracks how many times a user enters a negative number.
Build an accumulator that sums up a series of user-provided integers.

lectures.title: Working with Text
lectures.description: Focus on string manipulation and user interaction to make your programs more dynamic and communicative.

sessions.title: Strings and Indexing
sessions.description: You will learn how Python treats strings as sequences of characters and how to access specific parts of a string using indexes. You will understand zero-based indexing and negative indexing. This is the first step in learning how to parse and analyze text data.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to the conceptual core of text processing. In this public lecture, we begin by reframing what a 'string' actually is. Rather than seeing a word as a single blob of data, I want you to visualize it as a train with distinct carriages, or a row of lockers in a hallway. This mental model of a 'sequence' is the foundation of almost everything in Python. When we define a string like 'PYTHON', Python doesn't just store the word; it allocates a series of slots in memory, each holding exactly one character. This 'sequence' concept is the 'Why' behind our ability to manipulate text—if we can identify the position of a character, we can control it.

To bridge the gap to indexing, we must tackle the 'Zero-Based' hurdle immediately. I will draw a sequence of boxes on the whiteboard. Instead of labeling the boxes 1, 2, 3, we label the *offsets* or the boundaries. Think of it like a ruler: you start at 0 inches, not 1. This is a common stumbling block where beginners encounter 'Off-by-One' errors. I will explain that the index represents how many steps you are away from the start. Index 0 is the starting point (the first character), index 1 is one step away, and so on. This logical shift from 'counting items' to 'measuring distance from the start' is crucial for preventing index errors later in the course.

Next, we introduce the 'Negative Indexing' shortcut, which is a hallmark of Python’s developer-friendly design. I will visualize the string as a circular loop or simply show that while positive indices count from the left (the beginning), negative indices count from the right (the end). The 'Last Character' is always index -1. This is an elegant solution to a common problem: accessing the end of a sequence without needing to know its total length. I will demonstrate that `string[-1]` is the same as saying 'give me the very last carriage of the train,' which provides a massive boost in code readability compared to the manual math required in other languages.

We will pause for a 'Mental Execution' exercise. I will write a complex word on the board and ask you to identify the character at index 3 versus index -2. This isn't just about finding letters; it’s about verifying that your mental map of the memory slots matches Python’s logic. A frequent mistake here is trying to access an index that doesn't exist—like index 6 for a 6-letter word. I will use this moment to explain the 'IndexError', teaching you that the maximum positive index is always 'Length minus One' because we started at zero. This 'boundary awareness' is a professional habit that separates a coder who guesses from one who understands the underlying structure.

To wrap up, we will transition from static strings to user-provided text. By using the `input()` function, we turn these abstract index rules into a dynamic tool. We will walk through a script that takes any name and extracts the 'initials' or the 'tail' of the word. This reinforces that indices aren't just numbers—they are addresses. By the end of this session, you should view every piece of text not as a label, but as an addressable map of characters, ready for the slicing and transformation techniques we will cover in the next session.

tasks: Access the first and last characters of a user-provided string.
Identify the index of specific characters within a word.

sessions.title: Slicing and String Methods
sessions.description: This session covers extracting substrings through slicing and using built-in methods like strip(), upper(), and find(). You will be able to clean and transform text data efficiently. Mastering these methods will make your code more concise and professional.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by conceptualizing a string not as a static block of text, but as a flexible sequence of memory slots. Building on the previous session's introduction to individual indexing, we introduce 'Slicing' as the power to extract continuous segments. On the whiteboard, draw a long string like 'PROGRAMMING' with indices marked both above (0 to 10) and below (-11 to -1). The central idea here is the 'Interval' logic: Python slicing uses [start:stop], where 'stop' is exclusive. I will explain this by drawing physical 'cuts' between the characters rather than on the characters themselves. This helps prevent the common 'off-by-one' error where learners expect the stop index to be included in the result. By visualizing the indices as the boundaries between slots, the math of 'stop minus start equals length' becomes intuitive.

Next, we transition from the mechanics of slicing to the reality of 'Messy Data' using built-in methods. I will present a scenario where a user types '  Python  ' instead of 'Python' into a login field. This motivates the introduction of .strip(), .lower(), and .upper(). I want to emphasize that strings in Python are 'immutable'—they cannot be changed in place. On the board, I'll illustrate that calling text.upper() doesn't modify the original variable but creates a shiny new version of it. This is a critical conceptual hurdle: if they don't reassign the result to a variable (e.g., name = name.strip()), the 'cleaned' data vanishes. This explains why we often see 'chaining' like name.strip().lower(), which we will visualize as a factory assembly line processing a raw material into a finished product.

To bridge the gap between simple cleaning and searching, we introduce .find() and the concept of boolean checks within text. I'll ask the learner: 'How do we know if an email address is valid?' We look for the '@' symbol. This introduces the idea of 'String Inspection.' I will demonstrate how .find() returns an integer (the location) while the 'in' keyword returns a simple True or False. This distinction is vital for teaching them how to choose the right tool: use 'in' for a quick check, and .find() when you need to perform a precise 'surgical' operation, like slicing out the domain name from an email address.

We conclude with a 'Data Normalization' practice. I will provide a corrupted string like '###ERROR:User_Not_Found###' and challenge the learner to use a combination of slicing (to remove the hashtags) and methods (to lower-case the message). The goal of this exercise is to prove that complex text processing is just a series of small, logical steps. I'll watch for learners who try to hard-code the slice indices; I will then nudge them to think about how they might use .find(':') to make their slice dynamic, preparing them for the more advanced data-tracking tools they will build in the Unit 2 project.

tasks: Slice a string to remove the first and last three characters.
Use string methods to normalize user input (e.g., removing whitespace and changing case).

sessions.title: f-Strings and Formatting
sessions.description: You will learn the modern way to embed expressions inside string literals using f-strings. You will be able to format numbers and align text for clean output. This is vital for creating the user-friendly interface of your CLI calculator.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by conceptualizing the string as a 'container' for dynamic information rather than a static piece of text. I will start by drawing a hard-coded string on the whiteboard and contrast it with a scenario where variables like 'name' or 'price' are constantly changing. The goal is to move the learner away from the clunky and error-prone world of string concatenation (using plus signs) and into the elegant paradigm of string interpolation. I will visualize an f-string as a template with 'empty slots' marked by curly braces, explaining that the 'f' prefix tells Python to perform an active lookup of variables within those braces at runtime.

The core of the lecture shifts to the 'Colon Convention'—the hidden syntax that unlocks power within f-strings. I will draw a set of curly braces on the board and show how the colon acts as a separator: the left side identifies 'what' variable to display, while the right side dictates 'how' it should look. This is where I introduce float formatting. I’ll use the example of a shopping cart total (e.g., 19.99876) and demonstrate how ".2f" acts as a lens that rounds and truncates the display without modifying the underlying data. It is crucial to emphasize here that formatting is a 'presentation layer' concern; we aren't changing the math, we are changing the aesthetics for the human user.

To prevent the common mistake of forgetting the 'f' prefix or misplacing the colon, I will conduct a 'live-fix' exercise. I'll write a broken f-string on the board—perhaps one missing the prefix or one where the learner tried to put quotes inside the braces—and ask the class to predict why the program might crash or simply print the literal curly braces. This diagnostic moment helps learners understand that f-strings are specific instructions to the Python interpreter, not just fancy text.

We will then explore text alignment and padding, which is essential for the upcoming CLI calculator project. I’ll demonstrate how to use symbols like '>' or '<' followed by a number to create structured tables in the terminal. I’ll frame this as 'UI design for the command line.' By showing how to align a list of numbers or names into clean columns, the learner starts to see themselves as an engineer who cares about the end-user experience. We conclude by building a 'User Profile' snippet together that combines a string, an integer score, and a formatted float percentage, ensuring they see how different data types coexist harmoniously within a single f-string template.

tasks: Format a float to display only two decimal places within a string.
Create a dynamic message that greets a user and states their current score.

sessions.title: Input, Output, and Simple Programs
sessions.description: This session integrates all previous concepts to build interactive command-line programs. You will learn to handle the full cycle of input, processing, and output. This serves as the final preparation for Stage 1 of the course project.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by conceptualizing the computer not as a static calculator, but as a conversational entity. In this 'whiteboard' session, I will draw a simple feedback loop: Input -> Process -> Output. The core idea here is that a program is a black box that waits for human intent, transforms it, and returns a result. I'll explain that while code execution is fast, the 'input()' function is a unique moment of pause where the program yields control to the user. This establishes the psychological shift from writing scripts that just 'run' to writing software that 'interacts.'

I will then address the most common technical hurdle for beginners: the 'string-by-default' nature of user input. On the whiteboard, I'll illustrate how typing the number '5' into a prompt doesn't give the program an integer, but a piece of text. I'll use the analogy of a label versus an actual quantity. To bridge this, I'll demonstrate the necessity of 'type casting' or conversion—wrapping the input in 'int()' or 'float()'—before any math can occur. This is a critical diagnostic point; if a student forgets this, their 'plus' operator will concatenate strings (5 + 5 = 55) instead of adding values (5 + 5 = 10). I will deliberately show this 'bug' to trigger the intuition for data types we've built in previous sessions.

The narrative then moves to the 'Processing' stage, specifically how we use the text manipulation skills from earlier in this lecture to sanitize user choices. I will pose the scenario of a user typing 'ADD' versus 'add' or ' add '. I'll show how methods like '.strip().lower()' act as a 'cleaning filter' at the gate of our logic, ensuring our program is robust against human messiness. This transitions naturally into the concept of conditional branching—using 'if' statements to interpret that cleaned text as a command. This is the 'brain' of the program where the user’s string becomes an instruction for the machine.

To solidify these concepts, we will walk through the construction of a 'Stage 1 Calculator' and a 'Mini-Adventure.' During the practice phase, I’ll challenge learners to build a tool that doesn't just calculate, but communicates. I'll encourage them to use the f-strings we learned to provide descriptive results, like 'The total of your two numbers is {result}.' This reinforces the idea that the output should be as human-friendly as the input was. By the end of this session, the learner should see themselves not just as a syntax writer, but as a designer of experiences, ready to tackle the Unit 1 project with a firm grasp of the end-to-end data lifecycle.

tasks: Build a program that takes two numbers and an operator as input and prints the result.
Create a short interactive story program that branches based on user choices.

projects.stage_description: Create a script that uses variables and control flow to simulate a weather dashboard. It will accept user input for a city name and use conditional logic to provide clothing recommendations based on simulated temperature values.
projects.deliverable_increment: A single script 'weather_cli.py' that processes user input and outputs formatted text based on logic gates.
