lectures.title: Testing and Quality
lectures.description: Transition from writing code that works once to writing code that is verifiable and maintainable using industry-standard testing frameworks and type safety.

sessions.title: Writing Tests with pytest
sessions.description: This session introduces the pytest framework, teaching you how to write assertion-based test functions to verify code logic. By learning how to automate the validation of your logic, you gain the confidence to refactor code without fear of breakage, moving you toward professional-grade software development.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Begin the session by addressing a fundamental anxiety in programming: 'How do I know my code actually works?' Move beyond the manual 'print statement' debugging cycle that learners have relied on in previous units. Introduce the concept of the 'Safety Net'—automated testing. Explain that as our projects grow from simple scripts into the modular systems and class-based designs of Units 3 and 4, manual verification becomes impossible. The goal here isn't just to find bugs, but to build a suite of evidence that allows us to change code later without fear. This shift in mindset from 'writing code' to 'validating logic' is what distinguishes a hobbyist from a professional developer.

Transition to the whiteboard to visualize the relationship between the Source File and the Test File. Draw two separate boxes. Explain that Python looks for files prefixed with 'test_' to know where the validation logic lives. Use a simple 'add(a, b)' function as the first example. Write out the 'assert' keyword on the board. This is the most critical technical concept: the assertion is a boolean gatekeeper. If the statement after 'assert' is true, the program continues; if it's false, it raises an Error. Frame the test function as a formal question: 'I claim that when I give this function 2 and 3, it must return 5. Does it?' Use this to show how pytest automates the 'if result == expected' logic into a clean, readable one-liner.

Introduce the mechanics of the pytest command-line interface. Describe the visual feedback loop—the 'dots' for passes and the 'F' for failures. Explain why a failure is actually a victory for the developer: it’s the system catching a mistake before a user does. A common pitfall for beginners is writing tests that are too complex; emphasize that a test should be the simplest piece of code in the repository. If the test code is harder to understand than the source code, you've created a new problem rather than solving an old one. Demonstrate the execution process: saving the file, running 'pytest' in the terminal, and reading the Traceback to see exactly where the logic deviated from expectations.

Deepen the application by introducing the concept of 'Multiple Scenarios' or test cases. One test passing for '2 + 3' doesn't mean the function works for '0 + 0' or '-1 + 5'. On the board, create a table of 'Inputs' vs. 'Expected Outputs'. This visual helps learners organize their thoughts before writing code. Transition into a mini-practice where the learner writes three distinct test functions for a single utility. This exercise is designed to reveal the importance of coverage—ensuring the logic holds up under different conditions. Explain that by naming these functions descriptively (e.g., 'test_addition_with_negative_numbers'), the test suite serves as documentation for how the code is supposed to behave.

Conclude by framing pytest as an investment in the future. Explain that while writing tests takes time upfront, it saves exponential time during 'Refactoring'—a term the learner should now associate with cleaning and improving code. If the tests are green (passing), the internal logic is sound, even if we change the implementation details. This session sets the stage for the next topic on Edge Cases, moving from 'happy path' testing to 'defensive' testing.

tasks: Install pytest and write a test file for a simple mathematical utility function.
Execute tests from the command line and interpret the pass/fail report.
Create multiple test cases for a single function using different input values.

sessions.title: Edge Cases and Test Design
sessions.description: You will learn how to identify boundary conditions, such as empty inputs or extreme values, and design test suites that cover these critical failure points. Understanding how to break your own code through testing ensures your scripts are resilient in real-world environments where user input is unpredictable.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this session, the pedagogical focus shifts from the 'how' of testing syntax to the 'what' and 'why' of test design, specifically targeting the mental model of the 'Adversarial Developer.' The primary goal is to convince the learner that code is not 'done' when it works for the happy path, but when it is resilient against the extremes. We begin by visualizing a function as a physical bridge: it is easy to test it with a single car, but a professional engineer tests it for a hurricane, a structural defect, and an overweight truck. This transition from functional correctness to structural resilience is the hallmark of professional-grade software engineering.

We start the whiteboard visualization by mapping out the 'Input Space' of a simple function—for instance, one that calculates the average of a list of integers. I will draw a wide circle representing all possible inputs and then partition it. Most beginners stay in the center of the circle with lists like [1, 2, 3]. I will use the whiteboard to push them toward the boundaries: What happens if the list is empty? What if it contains a billion integers? What if it's not a list at all but a 'None' value? By visualizing these 'Edge Cases' as the physical boundaries of our code’s logic, the learner begins to understand that bugs almost always hide at the edges, where our assumptions about data types and sizes break down.

Next, we introduce the concept of 'Defensive Test Design.' I will explain that writing tests for edge cases isn't just about finding bugs, it's about defining the contract of the function. If we decide that an empty list should return 0, we write a test for it; if it should raise an Error, we write a test for that instead. This prevents the 'silent failure' trap—where a program continues running with incorrect data, leading to much harder-to-debug issues later. I will specifically address the common misconception that more tests are always better; instead, I'll teach the 'Equivalence Partitioning' strategy, showing how one test for a zero-value often covers a whole class of similar logic risks, making our test suite efficient rather than just redundant.

To bridge the gap to application, we will look at how to organize these tests using pytest markers. On the whiteboard, I'll demonstrate how to label tests as @pytest.mark.smoke (for basic functionality) versus @pytest.mark.edge_case. This isn't just about organization; it's about workflow. In a professional environment, you might run smoke tests every 5 minutes but run the heavy edge-case suite only before a major release. This introduces the learner to the reality of 'Test Suite Performance' and the strategic separation of concerns in a codebase.

Finally, the practice session will challenge the learner to 'break their own work.' By identifying at least three edge cases for a list-processing function, they are forced to move from a builder's mindset to a breaker's mindset. When they write specialized tests for null inputs and zero-values, they will likely see their original code fail for the first time. This 'Failure-First' moment is critical; it demonstrates that the test is working as a safety net, allowing them to refactor their logic with the confidence that they are building something truly robust.

tasks: Identify at least three edge cases for a function that processes a list of integers.
Write specialized test functions that specifically target zero-values and null inputs.
Use pytest markers or grouping to organize functional vs. edge case tests.

sessions.title: Code Style and Readability
sessions.description: This session covers PEP 8 standards and the use of linting tools to ensure your Python code is idiomatic and readable by others. Adopting professional styling habits is essential for collaboration in engineering teams and ensures your scripts remain maintainable as they grow in complexity.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by reframing 'code style' not as a matter of personal aesthetics, but as a technical requirement for long-term project survival. In a public lecture style, I start by presenting a functional but intentionally unreadable script—one with inconsistent indentation, single-letter variables like 'x' and 'y' for complex data, and no vertical spacing. The core idea to impress upon the learner is that code is read far more often than it is written. If a developer cannot scan a file and understand its intent within seconds, that code represents a 'tax' on every future contributor. I will introduce PEP 8 (Python Enhancement Proposal 8) as the definitive 'social contract' of the Python community, explaining that following these rules is what allows developers worldwide to step into each other's projects seamlessly.

The logic then moves into the specifics of naming and spacing as the two pillars of clarity. I will visualize the 'Naming Hierarchy': variables should be lowercase_with_underscores (snake_case), while classes must use CapitalizedWords (PascalCase). I'll point out a common beginner pitfall: using names that describe the data type (like 'list1') instead of the data's purpose (like 'user_emails'). By using better names, the code becomes 'self-documenting,' reducing the need for excessive comments. For spacing, I'll demonstrate how blank lines act like paragraph breaks in a book; they group related logical actions together and separate them from the next step, preventing the 'wall of text' effect that leads to logic errors during manual reviews.

To move from manual effort to automation, I introduce the concept of 'Linting' and 'Formatting.' I will describe a linter (like Flake8) as an automated proofreader that flags stylistic violations without changing the file, and a formatter (like Black) as an 'opinionated' tool that actually rewrites the code to meet standards. The key distinction to teach here is that while humans should understand the rules, we shouldn't spend our mental energy enforcing them manually. I'll describe the workflow of 'write-lint-fix' as a way to build muscle memory, eventually leading to a state where the developer writes PEP 8 compliant code naturally.

Finally, we transition to a refactoring exercise. I will provide a messy block of code and ask the learners to identify three violations before running an automated tool. This reveals the gap between what a human notices and what a machine catches. The goal is to show that even if the code 'works' (passes its tests), it is not 'done' until it meets the team's readability standards. I’ll wrap up by explaining that in professional environments, 'clean' code is a prerequisite for merging a pull request, tying these stylistic habits directly to their growth as software engineers.

tasks: Refactor a 'messy' script to comply with PEP 8 naming and spacing conventions.
Run a linter like Flake8 or Black on a project directory and resolve the flagged issues.

sessions.title: Type Hints
sessions.description: You will explore Python's type hinting system to explicitly declare the expected data types for function parameters and return values. This practice serves as 'living documentation' that helps IDEs catch errors early, aligning your workflow with modern Python 3 development standards.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by addressing a fundamental tension in Python: its dynamic nature is its greatest strength and its most dangerous weakness. In a concept-first lecture, we visualize the 'Contract of the Function'. Until now, a function has been a black box where we hope the user provides the right data type. We contrast this with Type Hints, which move us from 'hoping for the best' to 'explicitly declaring intent.' The primary goal here is to shift the learner’s mental model from viewing Python as a loose scripting tool to seeing it as a structured engineering platform where the code documents itself.

I will start by drawing a simple function on the board—something like `process_data(users)`—and ask the students, 'What is users?' Is it a list of strings? A dictionary of IDs? A custom object? Without Type Hints, we have to read the entire function body to guess. This leads into the 'Living Documentation' concept. I will demonstrate the syntax `variable: type` and `def function(...) -> return_type`. The emphasis isn't just on the colon and the arrow, but on how these symbols act as a contract between the developer and the IDE, allowing tools to catch bugs before a single line of code is ever executed.

Next, we move into the 'typing' module, which is where the power of modern Python 3 truly resides. I will introduce the concept of 'Generics' using `List` and `Dict`. I will explain that simply saying something is a 'list' isn't enough; we need to say it’s a 'List of Integers' (`List[int]`). This is a crucial distinction for preventing runtime errors where a string accidentally sneaks into a mathematical operation. We will also cover `Optional`, which is the most critical tool for handling the 'None' problem—a frequent source of crashes in production code. I'll frame `Optional[int]` as a way of telling the system: 'This might be a number, or it might be nothing; please be prepared for both.'

To bridge theory and practice, we will walk through a refactoring exercise. We take a 'messy' function that manipulates a nested dictionary and add complex type hints (e.g., `Dict[str, List[int]]`). During this, I will deliberately address a common misconception: that type hints change how Python runs. I must clarify that Python remains dynamic at runtime; these hints are 'ghosts' that the interpreter ignores but the developer cherishes. This sets the stage for introducing 'mypy'. I'll visualize mypy as a 'code auditor' that reads your hints and yells at you if you break your own rules. This practice moment is designed to show learners that type safety isn't a restriction, but a safety net that allows for faster, more confident development.

Finally, we wrap up by discussing the 'Advanced' tier of typing: Readability vs. Rigor. I'll show how over-typing can make code unreadable, and teach the 'Pragmatic Hinting' approach—typing public APIs and complex data transformations while leaving simple, obvious logic alone. We conclude by connecting Type Hints back to the earlier sessions on Testing and PEP 8, showing how a professional workflow integrates style, testing, and type safety into a single, cohesive shield against bugs.

tasks: Add type hints to a complex function involving dictionaries and lists.
Use the 'typing' module to define List and Optional types for function signatures.
Verify type consistency using a static type checker like mypy.

lectures.title: The Ecosystem
lectures.description: Learn to manage the external dependencies and environments that allow Python programs to scale and interact with the wider software world.

sessions.title: Virtual Environments
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to use venv to create isolated Python environments, preventing version conflicts between different projects. Master this to ensure that your development environment remains clean and that your scripts are reproducible across different machines.
sessions.sessionOutline:
The core conceptual hurdle of this session is shifting the learner's mental model from 'Python is a single program on my computer' to 'Python is a runtime engine that can support multiple isolated workspaces.' I will begin by framing the 'Dependency Hell' scenario: imagine one project requires Version 1.0 of a library, while a newer project requires Version 2.0. In a global installation, upgrading for the new project breaks the old one. This visualization of a 'cluttered house' helps learners understand that virtual environments (venvs) are not just a best practice, but a survival mechanism for professional scaling.

I will then transition to the 'Island Analogy' on the whiteboard. Each virtual environment is an isolated island. It has its own copy of the Python binary and its own 'site-packages' folder. When you are on Island A, you cannot see the tools on Island B. The key insight here is that the 'activation' step is simply a process of changing your system's PATH variable so that when you type 'python', it looks at the island's folder first. This demystifies the magic of activation scripts and prevents the common beginner mistake of thinking they need to reinstall Python itself for every project.

Next, we walk through the lifecycle of an environment: Creation, Activation, and Deactivation. I will demonstrate the command `python -m venv .venv`. I'll explain that '.venv' is just a folder name, but using a dot-prefix is a convention to keep it hidden and tidy. During the activation phase, I will specifically point out the change in the terminal prompt—the visual 'flag' that tells the developer which island they are currently standing on. This is a crucial moment to address a frequent stumbling block: the difference between shell types (Bash vs. PowerShell) and why the activation command differs slightly between them.

To solidify the concept, I will introduce a 'Verification' exercise. We will install a dummy package in the virtual environment and then attempt to import it from a global terminal window. When the global terminal throws a 'ModuleNotFoundError', it's a 'Eureka' moment for the learner—it proves the isolation is working. This prevents the misconception that packages are globally shared. I will conclude by emphasizing that venvs should never be committed to version control like Git; instead, they are ephemeral workspaces that we rebuild using metadata, setting the stage for the next session on package management.

tasks: Create, activate, and deactivate a virtual environment on your local system.
Verify that the environment has a unique set of installed packages separate from the global Python installation.

sessions.title: Installing and Managing Packages
sessions.description: You will learn to use pip to install third-party libraries and manage project requirements using requirements.txt files. This is a foundational skill for leveraging the vast ecosystem of open-source Python tools available for any specialized task.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this session, we transition from the concept of isolation to the concept of acquisition. I will start by visualizing the Python Package Index (PyPI) as a global warehouse of pre-built logic. The core intuition here is that a modern developer should rarely build everything from scratch; instead, they should act as an architect who integrates specialized tools. I’ll explain that 'pip' is the procurement officer of this warehouse. The most critical point to emphasize is that pip doesn't just download code; it resolves dependencies, ensuring that if Library A needs Library B to function, both arrive safely in your project. This prevents the 'it works for me' syndrome that plagues manual code sharing.

I will then move to the whiteboard to demonstrate the lifecycle of a package. We start with 'pip install', but I’ll deliberately pause to explain the difference between installing a package globally versus installing it within the virtual environment we created in the previous session. I’ll use the analogy of 'installing a kitchen appliance in a specific apartment vs. the building lobby.' This helps beginners avoid the common pitfall of polluting their system-level Python, which can lead to catastrophic OS-level errors later. We will visualize the path where these files live, reinforcing the idea that packages are just folders of Python scripts.

Once the learner understands how to get packages, I will introduce the concept of 'Reproducibility' through the requirements.txt file. This is the 'blueprint' of the project. I will frame 'pip freeze' not as a command to memorize, but as a 'snapshot' tool. By showing a snapshot of current dependencies and redirecting that output into a text file, I illustrate how we capture the state of our environment at a specific moment in time. This is the bridge to professional collaboration: you don't send your friend a 50MB folder of dependencies; you send them a 1KB text file that tells their pip exactly what to rebuild.

To prevent the frequent misunderstanding where students think 'pip install' and 'import' are the same thing, I will lead a brief exercise. We will install a library, and I’ll ask them to try and use it in a script without the 'import' statement, and then vice-versa. This clarifies the two-step process: acquisition (pip) and activation (import). The session concludes with a 'Clean Slate' drill where the learner creates a brand-new environment and uses their generated requirements.txt to recreate their workspace in seconds. This moment of automated setup usually provides the 'aha' realization regarding why professional developers are so disciplined about environment management.

tasks: Install a third-party library and generate a requirements.txt file using pip freeze.
Install dependencies into a new environment using a pre-existing requirements file.

sessions.title: Useful Standard Library Modules
sessions.description: We will take a deep dive into powerful built-in modules like 'datetime', 'collections', and 'pathlib' that solve common programming problems without needing external installs. Knowing the standard library well allows you to write more efficient and 'Pythonic' code by not reinventing the wheel.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing the Standard Library not just as a collection of tools, but as the 'batteries-included' philosophy that defines Python's utility. The core concept here is architectural efficiency: why would we import external weight when the language developers have already optimized solutions for common data patterns? I will start by visualizing the 'Standard Library' as the inner circle of the Python ecosystem—code that is already on the learner's machine, requiring no pip install, and guaranteed to be stable. This sets the stage for writing 'Pythonic' code that is lightweight and highly portable.

The first deep dive centers on 'pathlib' and the shift from string-based file manipulation to object-oriented path handling. I’ll contrast the old-school 'os.path' method (treating paths as mere strings) with 'pathlib.Path', where a path is a first-class object. The key intuition to build here is that a file path has behaviors—it can check its own existence, join itself to child directories, or read its own text. I will draw a 'Path' object on the board and branch out its methods like .exists(), .mkdir(), and the division operator (/) for joining. A common pitfall for beginners is forgetting that Path objects aren't strings; I’ll explicitly demonstrate why using the '/' operator is more robust than string concatenation, preventing the classic 'backslash vs forward slash' platform errors.

Next, we transition to the 'collections' module, specifically the 'Counter' and 'defaultdict'. The central idea is 'specialized containers for specialized logic.' I’ll use a frequency analysis example—counting words in a paragraph—to show how a standard dictionary requires manual checks for existence (if key not in dict...). By introducing the Counter, we simplify five lines of logic into a single instantiation. I want learners to see this as a mental shortcut: whenever you find yourself writing 'if key exists, increment, else set to zero,' you are reinventing a wheel that 'collections' has already perfected. We will pause for a quick exercise where learners use a Counter to find the most common element in a list, revealing how these objects provide high-level analytical methods like .most_common() right out of the box.

Finally, we tackle 'datetime', which is often a point of frustration due to the complexity of time zones and formats. I’ll teach this by focusing on the 'timedelta' object as the key to temporal arithmetic. Instead of trying to manually calculate how many seconds are in three days, we define a duration. The pedagogical goal is to move the learner away from 'math with numbers' and toward 'math with time units.' We will walk through a scenario of calculating a deadline: current time plus a timedelta. I will warn against the 'naive vs aware' datetime trap—explaining that time without a timezone is a floating concept—to prevent the bugs that occur when local scripts run on cloud servers in different regions.

The session concludes by synthesizing these tools. We’ll discuss a hypothetical script that finds all log files in a directory (pathlib), counts the error types within them (collections), and flags only those from the last 24 hours (datetime). This reinforces that these modules aren't just isolated tricks, but a cohesive toolkit for professional-grade automation that remains clean, readable, and dependency-free.

tasks: Use the datetime module to calculate the difference between two timestamps.
Implement a Counter from the collections module to analyze frequency in a dataset.

sessions.title: Popular Third-Party Libraries
sessions.description: This session introduces the heavy hitters of the Python ecosystem, such as Requests for networking and Pandas or NumPy for data, explaining when and why to reach for them. This overview prepares you to choose the right professional tools for specific engineering or data science objectives.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing the 'Batteries Included' philosophy of Python. While we've spent the previous session looking at the built-in standard library, the true power of Python—the reason it dominates modern engineering—lies in the 'Global Brain' of its third-party ecosystem. I'll visualize this on the board as a core nucleus (the language) surrounded by specialized orbits of libraries. The central concept here is 'Leverage.' I want learners to understand that for almost any complex problem—be it high-frequency trading, satellite image processing, or web development—a community of experts has already solved the 90% grunt work. Our job as engineers isn't to reinvent the wheel, but to be master curators and integrators of these specialized tools.

To move from the abstract to the concrete, I’ll categorize these 'Heavy Hitters' into functional domains. I'll start with 'Requests' for networking. I’ll pose a question: 'How would you manually handle HTTP headers, SSL certificates, and connection pooling?' The answer is that you shouldn't. By showing how `requests.get()` replaces hundreds of lines of socket-level code, I demonstrate the 'Intuition of Abstraction.' This is where I'll address a common beginner misconception: the fear that using libraries is 'cheating.' I'll reframe it as 'Efficiency'—professional developers are paid to ship solutions, not to re-write protocol handlers that have existed for decades.

Next, we pivot to the data and science tier: NumPy and Pandas. I will draw a distinction between Python's native lists and NumPy's contiguous memory arrays. The 'Big Idea' here is performance and vectorization. I’ll explain that while Python is easy to write, it's slow at heavy math, so we use NumPy (written in C) as a high-speed engine underneath. This leads into Pandas, which I’ll describe as 'Excel on Steroids.' I’ll visualize a DataFrame as a table that can handle millions of rows in milliseconds. This is crucial for students to see the scale difference between 'toy' scripts and 'professional' data engineering. We aren't just learning tools; we are learning how to handle data at a scale that manual processing could never touch.

Finally, we will touch on 'Application Frameworks' like Flask for web or Scikit-learn for machine learning. I’ll explain these as 'Architectural Blueprints'—they don't just provide functions; they provide a structure for your entire project. The practice moment here involves a discovery task: I’ll ask students to find a library for a niche interest (like 'BeautifulSoup' for scraping or 'Pillow' for images) and justify its use. This exercise is designed to reveal if they can identify the 'Problem-Tool fit.' The session concludes by demonstrating a live installation of one of these libraries into the virtual environment we created earlier, closing the loop from Unit 5's start: we create the environment, we manage the requirements, and now, we populate it with the world's best code to build something bigger than ourselves.

tasks: Research and present a brief use-case for three different high-profile Python libraries (e.g., Flask, Scikit-learn, BeautifulSoup).
Demonstrate the installation of one such library within a project environment.

lectures.title: Building Real Scripts
lectures.description: Synthesize everything you have learned to build interactive, automated tools that communicate with the internet and perform practical tasks.

sessions.title: Command-Line Arguments
sessions.description: You will learn how to use the 'argparse' module to create professional command-line interfaces for your scripts. This allows you to build flexible tools that can be configured by users at runtime, making your Python scripts feel like native system utilities.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by reframing the Python script from a static document to a dynamic system tool. The core concept to establish is the 'interface'—the idea that a professional script shouldn't require code modification to change its behavior. I will start on the whiteboard by drawing a diagram of a shell command, like 'ls -l /home', and decomposing it into the executable, the flag (optional), and the target (positional). This visual transition helps the learner understand that we are moving away from input() prompts, which pause execution and break automation pipelines, toward runtime configuration which is the industry standard for server-side and automation scripts.

Next, I will introduce the 'argparse' module as Python's standard engine for interpreting these terminal inputs. The mental model here is a 'Translator': argparse stands between the raw string the user types in the terminal and the internal variables the Python script uses. I'll sketch the four-step workflow on the board: importing the module, creating the parser object, defining the expected arguments, and finally, parsing the values into a namespace. The most critical point to emphasize is the distinction between positional arguments (required, order-dependent) and optional flags (using the '-' or '--' prefix). Beginners often struggle with why some arguments need names and others don't, so I will frame positional arguments as the 'noun' or 'subject' of the command, and flags as 'adjectives' or 'modifiers' that change how the action is performed.

To solidify this, we will dive into type validation and help generation. I will explain that argparse isn't just about reading strings; it's a defensive programming tool. By specifying 'type=int' or 'choices=['a', 'b']', we prevent our logic from ever receiving junk data, effectively moving our error handling to the very edge of the program. I'll demonstrate on the board how the module automatically generates a '-h' or '--help' menu, explaining that this isn't just a convenience for the user, but a professional standard that makes our tools self-documenting. A common mistake for learners is forgetting to handle the situation where a user provides no arguments; I will show how argparse handles this gracefully by default, providing a clear error message instead of a cryptic Python traceback.

Finally, we will move into the practice phase where the learner scripts a CLI tool that accepts both types of arguments. The goal of the practice tasks is to reveal whether the learner understands the lifecycle of an argument—from terminal input to a typed Python variable. By implementing help messages and custom types, they will see how a few lines of configuration can replace dozens of lines of manual string parsing and if/else logic. This session serves as the gateway to 'Real Scripts' because it elevates the code from a script that 'runs' to a tool that 'listens' and 'responds' to the execution environment.

tasks: Write a script that accepts optional and positional arguments from the terminal.
Implement help messages and type validation for CLI inputs using argparse.

sessions.title: Automating Everyday Tasks
sessions.description: This session explores combining file I/O, OS interactions, and logic to automate repetitive manual tasks like file renaming or report generation. Learning automation is the primary 'unlock' of Python fluency, enabling you to save time and reduce errors in your daily workflow.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by reframing the concept of a 'script' from a collection of syntax to a digital assistant. The core philosophy of this session is that automation is not about complexity, but about reliability and the delegation of boredom. I will start by visualizing the 'Manual Loop'—the physical act of a human clicking, renaming, and moving files—and contrast it with the 'Python Loop'. The goal is to move the learner from thinking about individual commands to thinking about 'Workflows'. We must establish the mindset that if a task takes more than five minutes and happens more than once a week, it is a candidate for a Python script.

To bridge the gap between abstract logic and the physical computer, we introduce the `os` and `pathlib` modules as the 'hands' of our script. The most important concept here is the 'Path Object'. I will explain why hardcoding strings for file locations is the fastest way to break a professional tool, especially when moving between Windows and Mac environments. We will visualize a directory as a tree structure in memory, using the whiteboard to show how Python 'walks' through branches. I’ll emphasize the 'Dry Run' pattern: printing what *would* happen before actually executing file changes. This prevents the common beginner disaster of accidentally deleting or misnaming a thousand files in a split second due to a logic error in a loop.

Next, we transition into the logic of pattern matching and bulk operations. The primary teaching beat here is the 'Filter-Transform-Commit' pipeline. First, we identify the target files (Filter); second, we calculate the new name (Transform); and third, we apply the change (Commit). I will walk through a scenario of renaming a messy folder of photos. This allows me to reintroduce string methods like `.replace()`, `.strip()`, and f-strings in a practical context. A common stumbling block is the 'Collision'—what happens if two files end up with the same name? I will teach the learners to anticipate this by adding 'Check-if-exists' logic, demonstrating how a professional script handles errors gracefully rather than crashing halfway through a batch process.

We then shift focus to 'Persistent Monitoring' through the creation of a system logger. This introduces the idea of 'Temporal Automation'—scripts that don't just run once and quit, but exist across time. I will explain the `time.sleep()` mechanism and its role in preventing a script from consuming 100% of the CPU. We will discuss the 'Append' mode in file I/O as the foundational logic for logging, explaining why we write to a file rather than just printing to a terminal: because logs are the 'black box' of software that help us debug what happened when we weren't looking. This connects back to the theme of building tools that work for us in the background.

Finally, we engage in a practice session where learners build a bulk renamer. I will look for students who forget to handle file extensions, as this is a classic oversight. The exercise is designed to reveal if they understand the difference between a filename and a file path. By the end of this session, the learner should no longer see their computer as a UI they interact with, but as an environment they can programmatically reshape, setting the stage for the next session where we extend this control to the entire internet via APIs.

tasks: Create a script that bulk-renames files in a directory based on a specific pattern.
Write a logger script that records system activity to a text file every minute.

sessions.title: Calling Web APIs
sessions.description: You will learn the basics of the HTTP protocol and use the 'requests' library to fetch and send data to web services. This session is critical for modern software development, as it allows your Python code to interact with the broader internet and external data sources.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by conceptualizing the internet not as a magic web, but as a giant conversation based on 'Requests' and 'Responses'. In a public lecture style, I will draw a whiteboard analogy comparing an API call to ordering at a restaurant: the client (our Python script) is the diner, the server is the kitchen, and the API is the waiter who carries the menu and the food. The central intuition here is that a Web API is just a function that lives on another computer, and our goal is to learn the syntax for calling it across the network using the HTTP protocol.

To make this concrete, we introduce the 'requests' library as Python’s most human-friendly way to speak HTTP. I will illustrate the structure of a GET request, highlighting the URL as the address and the headers as the 'metadata' of our message. The most important idea to convey is that when we hit a URL, we don't just get back text; we get back an object containing a status code, headers, and a body. I'll demonstrate this by performing a live fetch from a public JSON placeholder API, showing how a successful '200 OK' is the green light we need before we even touch the data.

Next, we tackle the 'Data Language' of the web: JSON. I will contrast a Python dictionary with a JSON string on the whiteboard to show they are siblings but not twins. The crucial teaching point is the 'serialization' gap—how we must use the .json() method to transform the raw bytes sent over the wire into a Python-native dictionary that our logic can actually manipulate. I’ll warn the learners about the common pitfall of trying to index into the response object directly without parsing it first, which usually leads to a TypeError. This is the moment where we bridge the gap between 'web data' and 'Python variables'.

Moving into robust engineering, we discuss the 'unhappy paths' of networking. Unlike a local loop, a web call can fail for reasons entirely outside our control—the Wi-Fi drops, the server is down, or the URL is wrong. I will teach the concept of 'defensive networking' using try/except blocks wrapped around the request call. We will specifically look at how to inspect the status_code attribute. I'll explain that codes in the 400s mean 'You made a mistake' (like 404 Not Found), while 500s mean 'The server is broken.' Teaching learners to handle these gracefully prevents their scripts from crashing silently or blowing up in a user's face.

Finally, we engage in a practice session where the learner must fetch data from an API and extract a specific nested value, such as a user's email or a specific post title. This exercise is designed to reveal if the learner understands the structure of the returned JSON and if they can apply conditional logic to handle a 404 error. By the end of this session, the learner should see Python not just as a calculator on their desk, but as a gateway to the entire world's data, capable of pulling live weather, stock prices, or social media feeds into their local scripts.

tasks: Perform a GET request to a public JSON API and parse the response body.
Handle common HTTP status codes (like 404 or 500) using try/except blocks and response attributes.

sessions.title: From Script to Small Application
sessions.description: In this final session, we discuss the transition from a single-file script to a structured application with tests, documentation, and error handling. This provides the roadmap for your final course project, ensuring you can package your work as a professional, shareable software asset.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by addressing the psychological shift required to move from 'writing code' to 'building software.' Up to this point, the learner has treated Python files like a series of instructions to be run in isolation. I will use the metaphor of a 'loose stack of papers' versus a 'bound book.' We visualize the messy state of a single script that has grown too large—where global variables clash and finding a specific function feels like a scavenger hunt. The goal here is to establish that project structure isn't just about tidiness; it's about cognitive load management. If a developer can't predict where a file lives, they cannot scale their ideas.

Next, we move to the whiteboard to map out the standard professional directory hierarchy. I will draw the project root and introduce the 'src' layout. It is crucial to explain the 'separation of concerns' by isolating the core logic in a source folder away from the metadata and configuration. We will discuss the roles of a 'tests' folder and a 'docs' folder, framing them not as chores, but as the 'insurance' and 'manual' that make the code usable by others (including the future version of the developer). I will explicitly warn against the common beginner mistake of putting test data or logs directly inside the source code folder, explaining how this pollutes the production environment.

Then, we tackle the orchestration of the 'main.py' entry point. This is where we revisit the '__main__' idiom from Unit 3, but now as a high-level conductor. I will describe how the main entry point should ideally contain very little logic; its job is to import modules, parse arguments via 'argparse' (connecting back to Session 1), and then trigger the heavy lifting. I'll visualize this as a 'Control Room' versus a 'Factory Floor.' The main script is the operator, while the modules in 'src' are the specialized machines. This distinction helps learners avoid the 'monolith' trap where they try to put everything in one file because importing across folders feels intimidating.

For the practice phase, we will simulate a scenario where the learner's automation script from Session 2 needs to become a distributable tool. We will perform a 'structural refactor' on the whiteboard before writing a line of code. The learner will identify which parts of their logic are reusable 'functions' and which are 'execution steps.' This exercise reveals if they truly understand modularity; if they struggle to separate their logic from their execution, it indicates a lingering confusion between definition and invocation. We will address this by showing how a well-structured project allows you to run tests on a single function without ever running the whole program.

Finally, we conclude by discussing the 'Professional Finish.' This involves the creation of a 'requirements.txt' file and a 'README.md.' I will explain that 'Software' equals 'Code + Metadata.' Without a list of dependencies or a guide on how to run it, the code is effectively broken for anyone else. This sets the stage for the final course project, emphasizing that they are no longer just solving logic puzzles, but are now engineering assets that can live and breathe in a production environment.

tasks: Outline a directory structure for a project including 'src', 'tests', and 'docs'.
Write a final 'main.py' that orchestrates functions from multiple modules to perform a complex automated task.
